name: Pentecost: the wind, the fire, and the three thousand
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The scene that opens Acts and starts the apostolic era. T1: on the day of Pentecost (fifty days after Passover), the eleven remaining apostles and about a hundred and twenty followers are 'all with one accord in one place' in a single upper room in Jerusalem (Acts 1:15, 2:1). T2: 'suddenly there came a SOUND from heaven as of a rushing mighty WIND, and it filled all the house where they were sitting' (Acts 2:2) -- a wind indoors, out of nowhere. T3: 'there appeared unto them cloven TONGUES like as of FIRE, and it sat upon each of them' (Acts 2:3) -- little flames, one per person, resting on each head. T4: they begin to speak in unknown languages, and the crowd in the street -- 'Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia, and Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome' (Acts 2:9-10) -- each hears the apostles speaking in his OWN native language. T5: PETER stands up with the eleven and preaches to the crowd; when he finishes, about THREE THOUSAND people are baptised that same day (Acts 2:41). Further rungs: some in the crowd sneer, 'These men are full of new wine' -- Peter opens his sermon by pointing out it is only the third hour of the morning, nine o'clock (Acts 2:13-15); Pentecost is the Greek name for the Jewish feast of Shavuot, which is why the city is full of pilgrims from every province.

name: Peter and John at the Beautiful Gate: silver and gold have I none
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The first named miracle of Acts, done at a doorway of the Temple. T1: Peter and John go up to the Temple 'at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour' (Acts 3:1) -- three in the afternoon. T2: at the gate of the Temple called BEAUTIFUL, a man 'lame from his mother's womb' is carried in every day and set down to beg alms of the people going in (Acts 3:2). T3: he asks Peter and John for money. Peter fixes his eyes on him and says, 'Look on us' -- and then the line: 'SILVER AND GOLD HAVE I NONE; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk' (Acts 3:6). T4: Peter takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and the man's feet and ankles receive strength; he goes 'walking, and LEAPING, and praising God' straight into the Temple with them (Acts 3:8) -- a grown man who has never walked, jumping. T5: the people who have seen him begging every day recognise him and are 'filled with wonder and amazement'. Peter uses the crowd to preach again, and this time about FIVE THOUSAND men come to believe (Acts 4:4) -- and Peter and John spend that night arrested in prison for it. Further rungs: the Beautiful Gate is traditionally identified with the Nicanor Gate of the Second Temple, made of Corinthian bronze that shone like gold; Peter's healing formula 'in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth' will be repeated across Acts as the mark of an apostolic sign.

name: Peter's chains, the angel in the cell, and Rhoda at the gate
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The jailbreak in Acts 12, told as a comedy of the miraculous. T1: King HEROD (Agrippa I) is persecuting the church; he has already killed James the son of Zebedee with the sword, and now he arrests PETER during the feast of Unleavened Bread and puts him in prison to be executed after Passover (Acts 12:1-4). T2: Peter is guarded by FOUR SQUADS of soldiers, four per watch, and inside the cell he sleeps chained BETWEEN TWO SOLDIERS, one on each side (Acts 12:6). T3: at night 'the ANGEL of the Lord came upon him, and a light shined in the prison: and he smote Peter on the SIDE' to wake him up. The angel tells him, 'Arise up quickly.' 'And his CHAINS FELL OFF from his hands' (Acts 12:7). T4: the angel tells Peter to get dressed and follow. Peter thinks he is dreaming. They walk past the first and second guards, and the IRON GATE that opens into the city 'opened to them of his own accord', and they go out and walk a whole street together -- and then the angel is gone (Acts 12:9-10). T5: Peter goes to Mary the mother of John Mark's house, where the church is praying for him, and knocks. A servant girl named RHODA hears his voice, is so astonished that she runs back inside to tell everyone WITHOUT opening the gate, and the praying disciples say she is mad -- 'It is his angel' (Acts 12:13-15). Peter is left standing outside knocking. Further rungs: Herod, unable to find Peter, kills the guards; not long after, sitting on a throne in a robe of silver at Caesarea, Herod is hailed as a god by the crowd, refuses to correct them, and is 'eaten of worms' and dies (Acts 12:20-23).

name: Stephen the first martyr and the young man Saul holding the coats
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The first Christian martyr and the moment that first names his future persecutor. T1: STEPHEN is one of seven men chosen by the apostles to serve at the daily distribution of food -- 'a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost' (Acts 6:5), the first named of the seven deacons. T2: brought before the Sanhedrin on charges of blasphemy, Stephen preaches a long sermon retelling the whole history of Israel from Abraham to Solomon (Acts 7:2-53), and ends by calling the council 'stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears' who have 'received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it' (Acts 7:51-53). T3: while they are gnashing their teeth, Stephen looks up 'stedfastly into heaven' and says: 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God' (Acts 7:55-56). The council put their fingers in their ears, and rushed him. T4: they drag him out of the city and STONE him. The witnesses (who by Mosaic law throw the first stones) LAY THEIR CLOAKS at the feet of 'a young man, whose name was SAUL' (Acts 7:58) -- the future Paul, on stage for the first time in the New Testament, at the killing of the first martyr. T5: as the stones fall, Stephen kneels and cries, 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge' (Acts 7:60) -- an echo of Jesus at Calvary -- and then he 'fell asleep'. Acts adds: 'And Saul was consenting unto his death' (Acts 8:1). Further rungs: the stoning scatters the Jerusalem church across Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1) and sets up the whole missionary sweep of the book; Stephen's name in Greek, Stephanos, means 'crown' -- the first crown of martyrdom in the Christian tradition.

name: The Damascus road: the light, the voice, and Ananias
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: Saul's conversion, the single most-painted event of Acts. T1: Saul is on his way to DAMASCUS, carrying letters from the high priest authorising him to arrest any Christians he finds there and bring them bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). T2: near Damascus at midday, 'suddenly there shined round about him a LIGHT from heaven'; he falls to the ground and hears a voice: 'SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?' (Acts 9:3-4). T3: Saul asks, 'Who art thou, Lord?' The voice answers, 'I am JESUS whom thou persecutest' (Acts 9:5). Saul stands up, opens his eyes, and cannot see; his companions have to lead him by the hand into the city. He is BLIND for three days, and neither eats nor drinks (Acts 9:8-9). T4: in Damascus, a disciple named ANANIAS is told in a vision to go to 'the street which is called STRAIGHT' and find Saul at the house of Judas (Acts 9:11). Ananias protests -- this is the man who has been jailing Christians -- but goes anyway, lays hands on him, and calls him 'Brother Saul'. Immediately 'there fell from his eyes as it had been SCALES: and he received sight forthwith' (Acts 9:18), and he is baptised. T5: Saul begins preaching in the Damascus synagogues -- his very first sermons, that Jesus is the Son of God (Acts 9:20). Local Jews plot to kill him, and the disciples let him down over the Damascus city WALL at night in a BASKET (Acts 9:25) -- Paul himself later brags about this: 'through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands' (2 Corinthians 11:33). Further rungs: Paul retells this scene twice more in Acts, before the Jerusalem crowd (Acts 22) and before King Agrippa (Acts 26), where he adds the extra line 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks' (Acts 26:14) -- the goads of a plough-ox.

name: The Jerusalem Council and the split of Paul and Barnabas
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: Acts 15 and the first great argument inside the church. T1: some men come down from Judea to Antioch and start teaching that Gentile converts must be CIRCUMCISED to be saved; PAUL and BARNABAS have 'no small dissension and disputation with them' and are sent up to Jerusalem to put the question to the apostles and elders (Acts 15:1-2). T2: at the council, PETER stands up and says the Gentiles have already received the Holy Spirit as they did at Pentecost; requiring the law would be 'a YOKE upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear' (Acts 15:10). T3: JAMES (the brother of Jesus, who has become the leader of the Jerusalem church) gives the decisive ruling: the Gentiles do NOT have to be circumcised; they need only avoid four things -- 'meats offered to idols, and from BLOOD, and from things STRANGLED, and from FORNICATION' (Acts 15:20). T4: the council writes a formal letter and sends it back to Antioch with Paul, Barnabas, and two others named JUDAS BARSABAS and SILAS -- the first church document, opening with the phrase 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us' (Acts 15:22-28). T5: not long after, Paul proposes to Barnabas that they revisit the churches they founded. Barnabas wants to take his cousin JOHN MARK. Paul refuses, because John Mark had abandoned them earlier at Perga; the CONTENTION is 'so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other'. Barnabas takes John Mark and sails to Cyprus; Paul takes Silas and goes overland through Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:36-41). Further rungs: John Mark, sidelined here, will later be the traditional author of the Gospel of Mark and a companion of Peter (1 Peter 5:13); the four Jerusalem-Council prohibitions echo the Noahide categories in later rabbinic tradition.

name: Paul at the Areopagus: the altar to the unknown god
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: Paul's most famous sermon, delivered to Greek philosophers on their own hill. T1: Paul is in ATHENS alone, waiting for Silas and Timothy, and his spirit is 'stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry' (Acts 17:16). T2: in the marketplace he argues daily with EPICUREAN and STOIC philosophers, who call him a 'babbler' and a 'setter forth of strange gods' -- and take him up to the AREOPAGUS (Mars' Hill), the ancient council-hill above the Agora, to hear him out (Acts 17:17-19). T3: Paul opens with a compliment. Walking through Athens, he says, he has seen many altars, 'and I found an ALTAR with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you' (Acts 17:23). T4: he then quotes their own poets to them -- 'IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND HAVE OUR BEING' (attributed to the Cretan poet EPIMENIDES) and 'FOR WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING' (from the poet ARATUS of Cilicia, Paul's home region) (Acts 17:28). T5: when Paul mentions the RESURRECTION of the dead, the Areopagus splits: some mock, some say 'we will hear thee again of this matter', and a few believe -- named specifically as DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE (a member of the court) and a woman named DAMARIS (Acts 17:32-34). Further rungs: Athens is one of Paul's smallest missionary hauls in Acts -- a handful of converts, and he leaves for Corinth; the sermon at the Areopagus becomes the model for every later attempt to preach to a philosophically educated pagan audience.

name: Paul and Silas: midnight singing, the Philippian earthquake, and the jailer's family
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The night jailbreak that plants the church at Philippi. T1: at PHILIPPI in Macedonia, Paul is followed for days by a slave girl 'possessed with a spirit of divination' who shouts after him and Silas in the street (Acts 16:16-17). Paul turns and commands the spirit out of her. Her OWNERS, furious that their income has just walked away, drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates. T2: the magistrates order them stripped and BEATEN with rods, then thrown in the inner prison, and their feet fastened in the STOCKS (Acts 16:22-24). T3: 'and at MIDNIGHT Paul and Silas prayed, and SANG PRAISES unto God: and the prisoners heard them' (Acts 16:25) -- two beaten men, feet locked, singing in the dark. T4: 'suddenly there was a great EARTHQUAKE, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's BANDS were loosed' (Acts 16:26). The JAILER wakes up, sees the doors open, thinks the prisoners have all escaped, and draws his sword to KILL himself before Rome does. T5: Paul shouts out of the dark -- 'Do thyself no harm: for we are all here' (Acts 16:28). The jailer calls for a light, runs in, falls trembling at their feet, and takes them back to his house; he WASHES their wounds, and then he and his whole HOUSEHOLD are baptised THAT SAME NIGHT (Acts 16:33). Further rungs: in the morning Paul refuses to leave quietly, revealing he and Silas are Roman CITIZENS -- 'they have beaten us openly uncondemned' (Acts 16:37) -- and the magistrates have to come in person to escort them out; Philippi becomes one of Paul's beloved churches (the epistle to the Philippians).

name: The silversmiths of Ephesus and the riot for Diana
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The mob scene in Acts 19, and the moment Paul's preaching threatens a whole industry. T1: Paul spends TWO YEARS teaching daily at EPHESUS in a lecture hall he rents from a man named TYRANNUS (Acts 19:9-10). So many people convert that magic-book owners bring their scrolls into the marketplace and BURN them publicly -- the value is counted at 'fifty thousand pieces of silver' (Acts 19:19). name: James the Just: the fuller's club at the Temple pinnacle

scope: The other James -- the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, dead at the same Temple where his younger relative had taught. T1: JAMES known as 'THE JUST' (or 'the Righteous') was one of the brothers of Jesus (Mark 6:3, Galatians 1:19). T2: the second-century Christian historian HEGESIPPUS (preserved in Eusebius, Church History 2.23) describes James's daily practice -- he was often in the Temple, on his knees so long praying for the people that his knees grew callused 'like a camel's'. T3: about the year 62 or 69 (accounts vary), the scribes and Pharisees demanded he stand on the PINNACLE OF THE TEMPLE and denounce Jesus to the Passover crowd below. Instead, James testified -- and they threw him down (Hegesippus in Eusebius, Church History 2.23). T4: he survived the fall. On his knees on the ground he prayed, 'I beseech thee, Lord God our Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' (Hegesippus) -- an echo of Jesus at Calvary. The crowd began stoning him. name: Peter crucified upside down at Rome
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The traditional martyrdom of the chief apostle, at the far end of the empire from Galilee. T1: after the Acts 12 escape and years of missionary work, tradition places PETER at ROME as head of the Christian community there; the letter called 1 Peter is written 'from Babylon' (1 Peter 5:13), which most ancient readers took as a coded name for Rome. T2: in the year 64, the great FIRE OF ROME breaks out under the emperor NERO. Nero, blamed for the fire himself, deflects the blame onto the Christians and begins the first Roman persecution (the historian Tacitus, Annals 15.44, records this without sympathy for the Christians and yet with disgust at Nero's cruelties). T3: Peter is arrested and condemned to CRUCIFIXION -- probably at the Vatican Hill, in Nero's private CIRCUS at the foot of the hill, where public executions were used as spectacle. T4: the church father ORIGEN, preserved in Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 3.1), records that Peter asked to be crucified HEAD DOWNWARD -- saying, as Jerome would later add, that he was not worthy to die in the same posture as Jesus. T5: he is buried nearby. Centuries later, the emperor Constantine builds a church over the traditional grave; that church is later replaced by ST. PETER'S BASILICA at Vatican Hill. In 1968 the Vatican announced that bones discovered under the altar were, in its view, likely those of Peter. Further rungs: the traditional date given by Jerome and Eusebius is that Peter died 25 years after coming to Rome; Peter's upside-down cross became a Christian symbol in its own right -- and, entirely separately, was later adopted by other groups as a mocking symbol, which is a modern confusion.

name: Paul beheaded on the Ostian Way
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The traditional death of Paul, twin to Peter's at Rome. T1: after his shipwreck at Malta and arrival at Rome (Acts 28), Paul spends 'two whole years in his own hired house' under a light form of house arrest, still preaching (Acts 28:30-31) -- the last scene the book of Acts gives us. T2: Christian tradition, unanimous from the earliest sources, is that Paul was executed at ROME under the emperor NERO, most likely between AD 64 and 67. Because Paul was a ROMAN CITIZEN, tradition says he was not crucified like Peter but BEHEADED with the sword -- the customary Roman capital punishment for a citizen. T3: the church father TERTULLIAN, writing about the year 200, is the earliest to state the execution method plainly, alongside Peter's: 'Rome, where Peter endures a passion like his Lord's, where Paul is crowned by the death of John' -- 'John' meaning John the Baptist, who was also beheaded (Tertullian, Prescription Against Heretics 36). T4: the traditional SITE is on the OSTIAN WAY (Via Ostiensis), the road that ran from Rome down to the port of Ostia -- specifically at a spot called AQUAE SALVIAE, today TRE FONTANE ('the three fountains'), where a later legend says his severed head bounced three times and a spring rose at each spot. T5: Paul is buried nearby along the Ostian Way. Constantine builds a church over the traditional grave, and today the ST. PAUL OUTSIDE THE WALLS BASILICA (San Paolo fuori le Mura) stands there -- with Peter's basilica at the Vatican, one of the two great apostle-tomb churches of Rome. Further rungs: the Roman festival of Saints Peter and Paul is kept on 29 June, remembering them together as the two founding apostles of the Roman church, though tradition says they were probably executed on different days in different parts of the city.

name: John on Patmos: the four horsemen and the woman clothed with the sun
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The last of the Twelve, the last book of the Bible, and one of the wildest visions in Western literature. T1: JOHN -- traditionally identified with the 'beloved disciple' who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper -- is the only apostle in the ancient tradition to die of old age. Under the emperor DOMITIAN (about the year 95), he is exiled to a small rocky island in the eastern Aegean called PATMOS 'for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ' (Revelation 1:9). T2: on Patmos, John sees a vision on 'the Lord's day' -- a voice 'as of a trumpet' behind him -- and turns to see a figure with 'his eyes as a flame of fire' and 'a sharp twoedged sword' from his mouth (Revelation 1:10-16), who dictates letters to seven churches in Asia (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea). T3: a scroll SEALED WITH SEVEN SEALS is opened one by one. As the first four seals break, the FOUR HORSEMEN of the Apocalypse ride out -- a WHITE horse whose rider carries a bow, a RED horse whose rider takes peace from the earth, a BLACK horse whose rider carries a pair of BALANCES, and a PALE horse 'and his name that sat on him was DEATH, and Hell followed with him' (Revelation 6:1-8). name: Andrew and the X-shaped cross of Patras
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The first-called apostle, and a cross that became a national flag. T1: ANDREW, one of the Twelve, is a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee and Simon Peter's BROTHER (John 1:40-42). T2: it is Andrew who spots the boy with the FIVE LOAVES AND TWO SMALL FISHES at the miraculous feeding, and brings him forward to Jesus (John 6:8-9) -- the small practical role that starts a famous miracle. T3: after Pentecost, ancient tradition (in Eusebius, Church History 3.1, drawing on Origen) sends Andrew missionary-preaching in SCYTHIA (the Black Sea coast north of Greece) and into the Greek region of ACHAEA. This later Byzantine tradition also names him as the first bishop of BYZANTIUM (later Constantinople), which is why the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople still today counts him as its founder. T4: at the city of PATRAS in Achaea he is arrested and condemned to death by the Roman governor AEGEATES. Tradition (the Acts of Andrew, and later Western sources) says he was crucified on an X-SHAPED CROSS -- called a saltire, or SAINT ANDREW'S CROSS -- either because he asked not to die on the same shape as Jesus, or by governor's choice. T5: Andrew's X-cross became one of the most famous heraldic symbols in the world -- the flag of SCOTLAND (a white saltire on a blue field, from Andrew's status as patron saint of Scotland), and part of the flag of the UNITED KINGDOM. name: Philip and Nathanael under the fig tree

name: Bartholomew flayed alive in Armenia
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The gruesome traditional death, and its most famous painting. T1: BARTHOLOMEW is one of the Twelve, paired always with Philip in the synoptic apostle-lists. Christian tradition (which the Nathanael ladder deals with) identifies him with the Nathanael of John's gospel. T2: ancient tradition (Eusebius, Church History 5.10, and later hagiography) sends Bartholomew as a missionary far east -- to INDIA (in one strand), and, in the stronger and later-dominant tradition, to GREATER ARMENIA. T3: at a city known as ALBANOPOLIS in Armenia, Bartholomew is said to have converted King POLYMIUS (a name not securely attested in the actual Armenian royal lists, so the tale is legendary rather than historical) -- which infuriates POLYMIUS'S BROTHER, Prince ASTYAGES, who orders Bartholomew's death. T4: the most famous version of the story -- preserved in the medieval Golden Legend and in Christian art since the Renaissance -- says he was FLAYED ALIVE (his skin stripped from his body while still living) and then BEHEADED. Other traditions have him crucified upside down like Peter, or beheaded outright; the FLAYING is the version that stuck. T5: MICHELANGELO, painting the Last Judgement on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in Rome (finished 1541), gave Bartholomew the most famous role: the apostle stands to the right of Christ, holding his own FLAYED SKIN in one hand and the KNIFE in the other. Michelangelo painted his OWN face on the flayed skin -- a self-portrait as a hollow hanging pelt. It has been called one of the most personal signatures in the history of Western art. Further rungs: Bartholomew's feast day is 24 August; he is the patron saint of TANNERS, LEATHER-WORKERS, and BUTCHERS -- trades that work with skin.

name: Matthew the tax collector at the receipt of custom
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The apostle called from a hated profession, and the painting that made his calling famous. T1: MATTHEW (also called LEVI in Mark and Luke) is a TAX COLLECTOR -- more precisely a publican, a man who has bought the right to collect Roman customs at a booth on the trade routes, and skimmed a living off the top. Jews of the period despised publicans as collaborators with Rome. T2: as Jesus walks along the shore of the Sea of Galilee near Capernaum, he passes Matthew sitting at the RECEIPT OF CUSTOM (Matthew 9:9) -- the customs booth. Jesus says two words: 'FOLLOW ME.' T3: Matthew stands up, LEAVES ALL, and follows him. Then he throws Jesus a great feast at his own house -- a house full of 'publicans and sinners' (Matthew 9:10, Luke 5:29). T4: the Pharisees complain to the disciples, 'Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?' Jesus answers, 'They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick ... for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance' (Matthew 9:11-13). T5: Christian tradition credits Matthew with the first-written of the four GOSPELS -- the gospel bearing his name, written originally (per the second-century bishop Papias, preserved in Eusebius Church History 3.39) 'in the Hebrew language' for a Jewish audience, later reaching us in Greek. In Christian symbolism the evangelist Matthew is represented by a WINGED MAN (or angel), from Ezekiel's four living creatures via Revelation 4:7. Further rungs: CARAVAGGIO'S painting 'THE CALLING OF SAINT MATTHEW' (finished 1600, in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome) shows Jesus's outstretched arm pointing across a dark tavern-like room at Matthew, who touches his own chest as if to say 'me?' -- one of the most famous religious paintings of the seventeenth century.

name: Judas Iscariot: the thirty pieces, the kiss, and the potter's field
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The betrayer, and two different ancient accounts of his end. T1: JUDAS ISCARIOT is one of the Twelve, treasurer of the disciples' shared purse (John 12:6, 13:29). At the Passover meal in Bethany, when a woman named Mary anoints Jesus with expensive ointment, Judas complains it should have been sold and the money given to the poor. T2: Judas goes to the chief priests and offers to hand Jesus over. Matthew names the price -- THIRTY PIECES OF SILVER (Matthew 26:15), the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32. T3: on the night of the arrest in the garden of Gethsemane, Judas comes with a mob of soldiers and gives Jesus the pre-arranged SIGN: 'Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast'. T4: MATTHEW'S account (Matthew 27:3-5) says Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, was 'seized with remorse'; he threw the thirty pieces of silver back down in the Temple, and 'went and HANGED HIMSELF'. name: Simon the Zealot and Thaddaeus: the two lesser apostles
strand: New Testament: apostles and early church
scope: The two apostles the gospels name and then barely mention -- and the traditions that grew up around them. T1: at the end of each synoptic apostle-list are two names that appear together: SIMON called 'the ZEALOT' (or 'the Canaanite', from the Aramaic word for 'zealous'), and JUDAS son of James, called THADDAEUS or LEBBAEUS in Matthew and Mark (Matthew 10:4, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15-16, Acts 1:13). T2: 'ZEALOT' meant something specific in first-century Judea -- the Zealots were a militant faction that wanted to drive Rome out of the Holy Land by force; several of them appear in Josephus's history of the Jewish revolt against Rome in 66-70. Whether Simon actually belonged to the Zealot party or was just personally 'zealous', the name is a striking pairing: a former militant sitting among former fishermen. T3: at the Last Supper it is THADDAEUS -- called 'Judas, not Iscariot' by John (John 14:22) -- who asks Jesus one of the great questions of the discourse: 'Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?'
